[Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188) 45 points by [ashriv](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=ashriv)[9 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188) | [hide](https://news.ycombinator.com/hide?id=50549188&goto=item%3Fid%3D50549188) | [past](https://hn.algolia.com/?query=Launch%20HN%3A%20Maritime%20%28YC%20F26%29%20%E2%80%93%20A%20managed%20cloud%20for%20production%20AI%20agents&type=story&dateRange=all&sort=byDate&storyText=false&prefix&page=0) | [favorite](https://news.ycombinator.com/fave?id=50549188) | [39 comments](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188) Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime ([https://maritime.sh](https://maritime.sh/)). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY) There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction: 1. Agent lifecycle management. There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up. 2. Custom environments. Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely. 3. Cost optimization. If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure. So what did we build differently? We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents. We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency. As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed. Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research. We want your feedback. If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build. Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing? Happy to answer any questions in the comments. [https://maritime.sh](https://maritime.sh/) [help](https://news.ycombinator.com/formatdoc) [agent_yard](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=agent_yard)[1 hour ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50554975) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50555326)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) The point about sandboxes being only a small part of the problem makes sense. Lifecycle seems like where most of the custom code ends up. Two questions: how do spend caps work when an agent gets stuck in a loop mid-task, do you stop it hard or let it reach a checkpoint first? And when a VM sleeps and wakes, what state is kept beyond the disk, for example open connections or in-progress tool calls? [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50554975&goto=item%3Fid%3D50549188%2350554975) [ashriv](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=ashriv)[14 minutes ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50555460) | [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50554975) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50555326)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Spend caps are enforced by us returning a 429 when a model provider is called, you can elect to have some sort of loop detection but that comes down to harness engineering - we don't touch what runs inside of the VM. In-progress tool calls are kept upon sleep/wake, however, open connections aren't (since typically the other side usually times out either way) [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50555460&goto=item%3Fid%3D50549188%2350555460) [aqibkhan026](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=aqibkhan026)[36 minutes ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50555326) | [prev](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50554975) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50550813)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) i've been looking into maritime, they're heavily customizable plus it has a really good sdk and interface if you want to integrate it with you existing platform. [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50555444&goto=item%3Fid%3D50549188%2350555444) [hmokiguess](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=hmokiguess)[7 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50550813) | [prev](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50555326) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50551892)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Forgive my naivety, but if it's built for agents then why should humans need to login, view a dashboard, care about it? Would there be a future where maybe the agent can elevate to the human what the human needs to know when it wants to or requires it from what it has access and these platform-like UX constructs are more like a "just in time" construct similar to Claude Artifacts? I expect the next cloud for AI to be fully headless, though maybe I'm wrong [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50550813&goto=item%3Fid%3D50549188%2350550813) [ashriv](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=ashriv)[6 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50551786) | [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50550813) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50549188#50551892)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) We are headless! The similarity is just colossal, it's what we built for ourselves and for our clients. articles.title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
articles.title_ko: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
articles.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

articles.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
articles.title_ko: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
articles.summary: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

articles.title: A System 1 Decision Model for Medical Multiple-Choice Questions Built on Frozen Language Models
articles.title_ko: A System 1 Decision Model for Medical Multiple-Choice Questions Built on Frozen Language Models
articles.summary: A System 1 model answers a multiple-choice question in a single pass. A frozen language model turns the question and each option into vectors, two small, trained heads place them in a shared space, and the closest option wins. The design has been shown on agent decisions, but we are not aware of a study of how far it goes on exam questions that need medical knowledge, where the right option is often no more similar to the question than the wrong ones. We rebuilt the recipe from scratch for MedMCQA and trained only two projection heads and one temperature on top of frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, Granite-4.2-3B and Qwen3-8B, using a contrastive loss with in-batch and hard negatives and a mask for repeated answers. With plain last-token vectors, both small encoders answer about one question in three correctly (33.1% and 33.0% on 3,842 held-out questions, where chance is 25.0%). Writing each text inside a one-word-summary prompt and lowering the learning rate of the heads raised this to 41.7% and 42.5% for the two small encoders and to 46.0% +-0.2 (three seeds) for Qwen3-8B. Shuffling the questions against the options returns accuracy to chance, so the heads do use the question. Flan-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2 report 57.6% and 72.3% on MedMCQA under a different protocol, so ours is a cheap, fast baseline and not a competitive system. We also say what our evidence cannot show: validation gains were about 1.7 to 2 times the test gains, and we could not separate the effect of reading several encoder layers from the other changes.
